keyTerms.definition: A thing's nature: what it is, that by which it is the kind of thing it is. For the Thomist it is what we grasp when we identify a thing's genus and specific difference.
keyTerms.example: The essence of a human being is (traditionally) rational animality; the essence of a triangle is being a closed plane figure with three straight sides.

keyTerms.definition: The fact or act of a thing's being real — not what it is, but that it is. For the Thomist it is not a property or accident, since a thing must exist before it can have properties.
keyTerms.example: Lions and unicorns have well-defined essences, but only lions have existence.

keyTerms.definition: A distinction that reflects a difference in mind-independent reality itself, not merely in the way we think or speak. It may or may not involve separability.
keyTerms.example: A dog and its leg are really distinct (and separable); a circle's radius and circumference are really distinct (but inseparable).

keyTerms.definition: A distinction that exists only in our words or concepts, with nothing in the thing itself corresponding to it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’: one reality, two phrases.

keyTerms.definition: Existing, but able not to exist; having existence not by one's own nature.
keyTerms.example: Lions exist but might never have evolved and could go extinct.

keyTerms.definition: Unable, even in principle, not to exist — existing by virtue of what one is.
keyTerms.example: Only something whose essence is existence itself would exist necessarily in this sense.

keyTerms.definition: In traditional logic and metaphysics (not modern biology), the more general class under which a kind falls.
keyTerms.example: Animal is the genus of human being.

keyTerms.definition: In the traditional sense, the more specific class within a genus, marked off by a specific difference.
keyTerms.example: Human being is a species of animal.

keyTerms.definition: The feature that distinguishes one species from others within the same genus.
keyTerms.example: Rationality distinguishes humans from other animals.

keyTerms.definition: The way members of the same species differ from one another: by being this parcel of matter rather than that one. Other differences (fur color, brain wiring) presuppose distinct matter.
keyTerms.example: Socrates is humanity plus this matter; Plato is humanity plus that matter — which is why neither is humanity itself.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's term for that whose essence just is existence: not one existing thing among others, but existence itself, subsisting on its own. It need not and could not receive existence from anything.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of the Thomistic proof; the one being that does not have existence but is existence.

keyTerms.definition: Causing an essence that is distinct from its existence to actually exist — adding existence to it, as it were.
keyTerms.example: Something must be imparting existence to Fido's essence right now for Fido to exist right now.

keyTerms.definition: The causal activity by which a thing is kept in existence from moment to moment rather than lapsing into nothing — as opposed to generation, which brings a thing into being from pre-existing materials.
keyTerms.example: Fido's parents generated him; what conserves him (and them, and their matter) in being now is a different question.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member causes only insofar as it is simultaneously being caused by a prior member, so that all but the first are merely instrumental. Such a series must have a first member.
keyTerms.example: C imparts existence to Fido only while B imparts existence to C, and B only while A imparts it to B.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes extended through time in which each member, once it exists, can act independently of earlier members. Such a series could in principle regress infinitely.
keyTerms.example: Fido from his parents, they from theirs, back through the generations.

keyTerms.definition: A cause whose causal power is entirely derived from something else in the very act of causing.
keyTerms.example: Every existence-imparting cause whose own essence is distinct from its existence is instrumental; it passes on existence it is itself receiving.

keyTerms.definition: Not the earliest cause in time, but the primary cause: one that causes without needing, in the act of causing, to be caused — the source on which every member of a hierarchical series depends.
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself imparts existence without receiving it.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's point that in a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence, essence is to existence as potency is to act: the essence alone is a merely potential thing; existence actualizes it.
keyTerms.example: Fido's essence by itself is a potential dog; with existence imparted, there is an actual dog.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality with no admixture of potentiality. Subsistent existence itself must be purely actual, since it has no potential for existence needing actualization.
keyTerms.example: The same being reached by the Aristotelian proof as the purely actual actualizer.

keyTerms.definition: Existence as expressed by the existential quantifier (‘there is an x such that x is F’) — a second-order predicate of concepts, saying a concept has instances. Associated with Frege.
keyTerms.example: ‘Cats exist’ = something falls under the concept cat.

keyTerms.definition: Existence as something true of an individual — what a thing has while it lasts and loses when destroyed. Corresponds to Frege's Wirklichkeit.
keyTerms.example: The Great Pyramid still has it; the Library of Alexandria lost it.

keyTerms.definition: Knasas's point that we grasp the subject of an existential statement without already presupposing that it exists or doesn't, so ‘Martians do not exist’ is not self-contradictory even if existence is predicated of things.
keyTerms.example: ‘Martians do not exist’ = Martians, which of themselves are neutral as to existence, are not in fact real.

keyTerms.definition: The logical rule that co-referring terms can be swapped without changing truth value — which fails in contexts of knowing or believing.
keyTerms.example: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, but I may know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does.

keyTerms.definition: Two concepts are logically independent when fully grasping one does not bring knowledge of the other. Klima uses this to show why the lion case differs from the aspirin case.
keyTerms.example: Fully grasping aspirin's chemical essence brings knowledge that it is acetylsalicylic acid; fully grasping a lion's essence never brings knowledge that lions exist.

keyTerms.definition: The thesis that at least some things, especially natural substances, have real, mind-independent essences — not to be confused with the rationalist ‘essentialism’ Gilson criticized.
keyTerms.example: Copper, oaks, and polar bears have natures discovered, not invented, by us.

keyTerms.definition: The view that all essences are products of human concepts, language, or purposes. Feser (following Crawford Elder) argues it is incoherent when applied to the mind itself.
keyTerms.example: Artifacts like can openers have conventional essences; the conventionalist says everything does.

keyTerms.definition: Wrongly inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do. Feser argues part-to-whole inferences are not always fallacious and that the Thomistic proof doesn't rely on one anyway.
keyTerms.example: Each brick weighs a pound, so the wall weighs a pound (fallacious); each Lego brick is red, so the wall is red (valid).

keyTerms.term: De Ente et Essentia (On Being and Essence)
keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's early treatise, chapter 4 of which is the classic source of the reasoning behind the Thomistic proof and of the phrase ‘subsistent existence itself’.
keyTerms.example: Feser cites it when introducing ipsum esse subsistens.

distinctions.name: Essence vs. existence

left.label: Essence (what it is)
left.desc: The nature a thing has — the answer to ‘What is it?’ Fully describable without settling whether any such thing is real (lions, pterodactyls, unicorns).

right.label: Existence (that it is)
right.desc: The fact or act of being real — the answer to ‘Is there any?’ Known only by experience (a posteriori) in the case of the things around us, never read off the essence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The whole proof rests on this contrast. If existence were part of what things are, they would need no cause of their being; because it isn't, they must receive existence from outside.

distinctions.name: Real distinction vs. merely conceptual (verbal) distinction

left.label: Merely conceptual
left.desc: Two ways of thinking or speaking about one and the same reality, like ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’, or (the critic claims) ‘aspirin’ and ‘acetylsalicylic acid’.

right.label: Real
right.desc: Two aspects that differ in mind-independent reality, whether or not they can be separated.

distinctions.whyItMatters: If essence and existence differed only in our concepts, a thing's existence might be ‘built into’ it after all, and no cause of existence would be required. Feser's three arguments and Klima's reply to the aspirin objection defend reality here.

distinctions.name: Distinct-and-separable vs. distinct-but-inseparable

left.label: Separable real distinction
left.desc: Things that can exist apart: two dogs; a dog and its leg.

right.label: Inseparable real distinction
right.desc: Aspects that can never occur apart yet are not the same: a circle's radius and circumference; triangularity and trilaterality; a thing's essence and its existence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Kenny's objection assumes that real distinction requires separability. Showing that it doesn't disarms him — and also shows why ‘they're inseparable’ doesn't explain why essence and existence are united.

distinctions.name: Incomplete conception vs. misconception

left.label: Incomplete conception
left.desc: Missing part of a thing's essence without denying it: knowing a lion is an animal but not yet that it is a cat.

right.label: Misconception
right.desc: Denying something that belongs to the essence: judging that a lion is not a cat.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Denying that lions exist is a false judgment but not a misconception of what a lion is. That shows existence is not part of a lion's essence, answering the charge that we just haven't grasped the essence completely.

distinctions.name: Linear (generating) series vs. hierarchical (conserving) series

left.label: Linear / per accidens
left.desc: Causes spread out in time, generating new things from pre-existing materials; each member can act independently once it exists (Fido's ancestry). Could in principle be infinite.

right.label: Hierarchical / per se
right.desc: Simultaneous causes, each imparting existence only insofar as it is right now receiving existence from a prior one. All but the first are instrumental; must have a first member.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’ and the ‘what about an eternal universe?’ objection both target linear series. The Thomistic proof is entirely about the hierarchical series of conservation.

distinctions.name: Having existence vs. being existence

left.label: Having existence (esse receptum)
left.desc: A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence: it is a potential that has been actualized, needs a cause, can be many, is contingent.

right.label: Being existence (ipsum esse subsistens)
right.desc: That whose essence just is existence: needs and could have no cause, is unique, necessary, purely actual.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is why the proof's first cause is not an ad hoc exception to a causal rule: the rule applies only to what has existence, and the first cause is what is existence. And it is why there is no middle ground: existence as a ‘part’ of an essence collapses into essence being existence.

distinctions.name: Specific existence vs. individual existence (Kenny)

left.label: Specific existence
left.desc: ‘There is an x such that x is F’ — a concept's having instances; a second-order predicate of concepts (Frege).

right.label: Individual existence
right.desc: What an individual has while it lasts and loses when destroyed (Great Pyramid vs. Library of Alexandria); Frege's Wirklichkeit.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Kenny argues the real distinction fails on either reading. The Thomist replies that Kenny assumes separability, assumes these are the only respectable notions of existence, and ignores the further question of what makes a concept be instantiated at all — which is the Thomist's act of existence.

distinctions.name: First in time vs. first in the order of dependence

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest cause in a sequence stretching back into the past — the cause a ‘beginning of the universe’ argument is after.

right.label: Primary (ontologically first)
right.desc: The cause on which every other member depends right now for its causal power — even if (per impossibile) the series were infinite.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The Thomistic proof's ‘first cause’ is primary, not temporally first. That is why it is compatible with an eternal universe or multiverse.

illustrations.title: Lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns
illustrations.body:
Describe three creatures in full biological detail to someone who has never heard of them. Then tell him: one of these is alive today, one is extinct, one never existed — which is which? No amount of study of the descriptions will tell him. The essences are fully on the table, but existence is not among the items listed.

Use it to show that **what a thing is** leaves open **whether it is**. Then add the follow-up: denying that lions exist would be a mistake about the world, not a misunderstanding of what a lion is.

illustrations.title: Bachelors and unmarried men
illustrations.body: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ are two expressions for exactly one reality — nothing in any bachelor answers to the difference in wording. Feser uses this as the model of a *merely verbal* distinction, to sharpen the question: is essence vs. existence like this, or does it mark something in things themselves?

illustrations.title: The circle's radius and circumference
illustrations.body:
Every circle has a radius and a circumference, and you will never find one without the other. Yet they are obviously not the same thing — one is 2π times the other. They are **really distinct but inseparable**, and both follow from the essence of a circle. The same goes for having three angles and having three sides.

This example does double duty: it shows that a real distinction need not mean separability (answering Kenny), and it shows what essence and existence *lack* — existence does not follow from a lion's essence the way the circumference follows from the circle's.

illustrations.title: Fido blinking out
illustrations.body:
Fido's parents explain how he got started. But right now, this instant, Fido's existence is still not part of what a dog is, and Fido cannot be supplying it to himself (he would have to exist already in order to do anything). So something must be imparting existence to him now — otherwise he would simply blink out, no more real than before he was conceived.

Use Fido to shift the listener's imagination from **how things began** to **what keeps them in being**.

illustrations.title: An infinite stack of IOUs
illustrations.body: An IOU is only worth something if, somewhere, it is backed by real money. Pile up IOUs that point to other IOUs, even infinitely many, and you still have no money. A chain of causes each of which only *passes on* existence it is itself receiving is like that: however long, it yields no real dog unless it is backed by something that has existence not on loan but by nature — subsistent existence itself.

illustrations.title: Socrates is not humanity
illustrations.body: Socrates and Plato are both fully human, yet they are two. What makes them two is that each is humanity *plus* a distinct parcel of matter — which is exactly why neither of them *is* humanity itself. Now try to make two things that are each *existence itself*: whatever you add to distinguish them (a specific difference, a parcel of matter, anything) makes each ‘existence itself plus something’, which is no longer existence itself. So there can be only one.

illustrations.title: Red Lego wall vs. heavy brick wall
illustrations.body: Each brick weighs a pound; the wall doesn't. But each Lego brick is red; the wall is red. Some part-to-whole inferences fail and some succeed, so ‘fallacy of composition’ is not a magic word. And in any case the Thomistic proof never needs the inference: one dog is enough to get to subsistent existence itself.

illustrations.title: Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid
illustrations.body: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, yet a person with a hazy grasp of aspirin can know it relieves pain without knowing it is acetylsalicylic acid. The critic says the lion's essence and existence might be like that: one reality, two concepts. Klima's reply: if you grasped aspirin's chemical essence *completely*, you couldn't miss that it is acetylsalicylic acid. But no complete grasp of what a lion is would ever tell you that lions exist. The concepts of aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are not logically independent; the concepts of a lion and a lion's existence are.

illustrations.title: A recipe is not a dinner
illustrations.body: A recipe tells you exactly what a dish is — ingredients, proportions, method. You can own a thousand recipes and still be hungry: none of them contains a meal. A recipe is a *potential* dinner; something else must make it actual. An essence is like the recipe; existence is the meal being real. (Unlike a recipe, of course, an essence is not an object on its own — it only ever exists as the essence of an existing thing; the analogy is about the gap between specification and reality.)

illustrations.title: The picture on a screen
illustrations.body: An image on a monitor is there only while the signal is continuously being sent; cut the signal and the picture doesn't linger, it vanishes. Compare a statue, which stays put after the sculptor leaves. The Thomistic claim is that, with respect to *existence itself*, everything is like the screen image rather than the statue: its being is continuously received. Use this to explain conservation — but add that the ‘signal source’ in the proof, unlike any transmitter, is not itself receiving power from anything further.
